svg.title: What is published, and what this paper adds
svg.desc: Layered diagram on one page. The base is Hixson and Guliani's 2015 frame [6]: organic and inorganic growth; a planning horizon at least as long as resource order time; fungibility; planning for only some launches, with a correlation check; a lead-time table ending at "Ready to serve," step 2 in outline; weighting actions with "costs" so they normalize into one driver, an early form of this paper's coefficient; checking that blow-up factors "remain accurate" and writing down design assumptions, the same idea as a valid range; keeping step changes itemized to "learn as you repeat the process," which scoring by stage writes down; "That tolerance should define how aggressively you provision," the shortage-to-idle choice; the "sensitivity" of estimates "to their time horizon," the residual uncertainty at a commit point; shorter lead times as among "the most valuable things" a company can do; and a Plan B for a "success disaster." Above it, three published families are placed by when they decide: statistical driver regression after observing history [13]; coefficient graphs and attribution each planning cycle [1, 2, 14]; priced allocation before resources are assigned [15–18]. A side column notes that step-change demand is declared by the team that knows it, runs optimistic and can be checked against a reference class [7, 8–10, 30–34]. Above that, a band lists some parts borrowed from operations, finance and IT management: hierarchical planning, gain-sharing and IT financial management [3–5]; parties and stages [19–24]; Olavson's base-and-high consensus, customer-versus-statistical check, slow layers planned to a high quantile and quantiles varying by component [8]; netting and time fences, standard manufacturing practice; and the operations results named with the sections that cite them: the newsvendor formula (Section 6.3); postponement, quantity flexibility, chained flexibility and the option value of waiting (Section 6.2). Others are cited where the text uses them. The top band shows what this paper adds: a rule tying each supply layer's commitment to the declaration's stage at its commit point, and governance with owners, versions and ledgers, with a sub-line: ratios are monitored in [7]; owners, versions and restatement are added here. A note says the coefficient-as-agreement claim extends Meta's "capacity contracts" [31] from the amount of capacity to the coefficient and rate. A card in the published band credits the 2026 SRE chapter [7], by Gordon, Kirby, Hixson and colleagues: planned and unplanned inorganic demand, percentile forecasts and backtesting, an unconstrained plan turned into a plan of record, pooling, stranded capacity, and demand and supply shaping; supply dimensions (fungibility, lead time, elasticity); phased, non-binary readiness. A bracket marks it as the same lineage as the 2015 frame.
